intro: Melbourne Beach owes little: $469,000 of loans at the end of its last audit, and its stormwater loan was paid off in July 2026. Now it is asking voters whether to borrow $5.0 million for stormwater and roads. This page lays out the arithmetic of borrowing and of saving, using the town’s own numbers.
notice: Melbourne Beach voters decide the bond on November 3, 2026. This site takes no side. It shows the town’s own figures, the arithmetic both ways, and the town’s own reasons — and opens no vote on the question.

forward.title: The $5.0 million question, both ways
forward.lead: The ballot asks to borrow up to $5,000,000, repaid over up to 20 years from property taxes. The town estimates the cost at 0.53 to 0.70 mills a year — $131 to $175 a year on a home with $250,000 of taxable value. On today’s taxable value ($725,977,934), that is about $385,000 to $508,000 a year.
points: Borrow: about $385,000–$508,000 a year for 20 years is $7.7–$10.2 million in all at today’s values — so roughly $2.7–$5.2 million of it would be interest. The town hasn’t said what interest rate its estimate assumes (Docket #5).

Save first: setting aside the same $385,000–$508,000 a year would reach $5.0 million in about 10 to 13 years, if interest earned only keeps up with rising construction costs. Nothing gets built until then.

Use savings: the town held $5.7 million in its bank accounts on July 31, 2026, and its General Fund had $3.5 million unassigned — 78% of a year’s spending. The town says it wants to keep reserves as security “against uncertainties such as hurricanes.”

The town’s case for borrowing, in its own words: several needs “can no longer be deferred,” costs rise every year a repair waits, and a bond “spreads the costs to all who will benefit” over the 15–25 year life of the projects.
If the bond fails, the town says the Commission would “revisit the project list, pursue an alternative financing mechanism or fund projects incrementally through the annual operating budget.”
